name: Candidacy article
reach: the Journal page, which is under About in the menu at the top; it is the last of the six guides listed there, and four of the Where it hurts pages link to it
purpose: Tells a patient plainly who tends to be considered for this care, who is sent back to their specialist, and how a clinician makes the decision on a video call. It exists so nobody books expecting a yes that the practice cannot honestly give.
owner_notes: This is the site's fullest answer to who is a candidate. It lists who tends to be considered and who is sent back to their specialist, and says the decision is a clinical judgement made on the consultation, never by the page.
It says the clinician gives one of three answers: yes, with a written plan; no, with the reason; or more information is needed first.
It links to the two-minute fit check on the Home page, which gives no score and sends nothing anywhere.
Four Where it hurts pages link here under The science, if you want it: After an injury, Back and neck, Before surgery and Hips. The article on surgery questions links here too.
replace: The reviewer line under the heading: your own clinical reviewer's name and the review date replace the sample {{site.reviewer.name}}.
The last source at the end, Clinic candidacy criteria, is stamped Sample: your own clinician adds your criteria before launch.
The two lists, who tends to be considered and who is sent back, are sample wording: your own clinician reviews them before launch so they match how your practice decides.
The closing band at the bottom: your phone number replaces the sample {{site.phone}}.
keep: The sentence that regenerative therapy is investigational for most musculoskeletal uses and is not FDA-approved to treat any orthopedic condition.
The sentence that candidacy is a clinical judgement made by a licensed clinician on the consultation, never by the page.
The line that the practice cannot offer a certain outcome and will not pretend to.
The honest expectation, in the part about the written plan, that individual results vary.

The small print at the bottom: statements not evaluated by the FDA, not FDA-approved and investigational for most uses, individual results vary, and the California notice unless your own lawyer confirms it does not apply.

top.say: The top of the article says a good clinic tells some people no, and shows who reviewed it; the reviewer on this example is a sample name.

article.say: The article itself lists who tends to be considered and who is sent back to their specialist, then explains how a clinician decides on the video call.

questions.q: What is the candidacy article for?
alt: What does the article on who is a candidate do?
Why does my site say who isn't a candidate?
questions.say: It tells a patient plainly who tends to be considered and who is sent back to their specialist. It also explains how the decision is made: by a licensed clinician, on a video call, never by the page. Saying no openly is part of what makes your site believable.

questions.q: Where does the site say who is not a candidate?
alt: Where is the list of people you send back?
Where does it say who this is not for?
questions.say: In the Journal, in the guide called Who is, and isn't, a candidate. Open the menu at the top, choose About, then Journal, and it is the last of the six. The list is headed Who we send back to their specialist.

questions.q: Who does the site say gets sent back to their specialist?
alt: Who does the site turn away?
Who is this care not for?
questions.say: The article lists four groups, and these are the main three. Someone with an active infection, or cancer under active treatment, is asked to see their own physician first. A joint that has lost its structure goes to a surgeon, and anyone wanting a promised outcome is told the practice cannot offer one.

questions.q: What do I change on the candidacy article?
alt: What do I replace on the candidacy article?
Are the candidacy rules mine to set?
questions.say: Two spots are stamped Sample. The reviewer line at the top takes your own clinician's name and date; on this example it shows {{site.reviewer.name}}, a sample name. The last source at the end is where your clinician adds your own criteria. Your clinician also reads the two lists before launch.

questions.q: How is it decided whether I'm a candidate?
alt: Can you tell me if this is for me?
Can you tell a patient whether they qualify?
questions.say: A licensed clinician decides, on a video call, never the page and never me. The article says they look at your history, your imaging and your goals. You hear one of three answers: yes with a written plan, no with the reason, or more information is needed.

questions.q: What is in the written plan?
alt: What do I get if the answer is yes?
questions.say: The article says it sets out the treatment and where the product comes from, who gives it and who oversees it, and the full cost. It also gives the follow-up schedule and says plainly that results vary. You take it away and decide in your own time.
